notes.quote: וְ⁠רִבְקָ֣ה שֹׁמַ֔עַת בְּ⁠דַבֵּ֣ר יִצְחָ֔ק אֶל־עֵשָׂ֖ו בְּנ֑⁠וֹ
notes.text: Your language may have its own term or expression for this relationship. The phrase **his son** probably recalls the fact that Esau was Isaac’s favorite son (Genesis 25:28). or [Rebecca listened to what Isaac said as he spoke to his son Esau]
In Hebrew, the word for “hand” is the same word as for “arm.” Isaac probably felt Esau’s hands and arms.

It was a Hebrew custom for relatives and close friends to greet each other with a kiss on each cheek. Also consider whether it is more natural in your language to put the address **my son** first in this quote.

In the Hebrew text, **you** is singular in verses 28–29 and refers to both Jacob and his descendants. If necessary, you could make that explicit in your translation. or [I pray that God will give you and your descendants]

Isaac knew from what Esau just said in verse 31 that one of his sons was talking to him. Also, Isaac is very upset, so some translations add an exclamation point after the question mark to help communicate that.

The expression **he will be blessed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. or [Then I asked God to bless him, so God will definitely bless him]

notes.quote: הֲ⁠כִי֩ קָרָ֨א שְׁמ֜⁠וֹ יַעֲקֹ֗ב וַֽ⁠יַּעְקְבֵ֨⁠נִי֙ זֶ֣ה פַעֲמַ֔יִם
notes.text: Esau uses a rhetorical question here to show his strong emotion. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. To help readers understand why Esau said this about Jacob, you could include a footnote such as the following: The name **Jacob** means “heel-grabber” and can imply deception. He was given that name because when he was born he was grabbing hold of Esau’s heel (Genesis 25:26).

The phrase **live by your sword** is an idiom that means Esau and his descendants will have violent conflict with others, often in order to survive. or [You and your descendants will continually be fighting battles with other peoples]

notes.topic: break his yoke off of your neck
notes.text: The verbal image **break his yoke off of your neck** means that Esau and his descendants will be free from the control of Jacob and his descendants. A yoke is a wooden collar that is placed around the necks of work animals to control them as they pull a plow or cart. or [you will no longer be under his rule]

The author is repeating forms of the verb **blessed** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. or [because their father had blessed Jacob instead of him]
In that culture, they had the custom of mourning the death of a loved one for a certain period of time, anywhere from a week to a month or more.

Consider whether it is more natural in your language to end this sentence here or to continue the sentence into verse 45. Also, the phrase **turns away** is used here as an idiom that means “becomes less” or “goes away.”
Notice that the Hebrew word for **anger** here is different from the stronger word **fury** in verse 44. or [After a while, when your brother is no longer angry with you]
To show that Rebekah is speaking with strong emotion, you could use an exclamation point at the end of this sentence and the following one.
